article: Identifying River Rocks by Color, Pattern, and Density

images.caption: Granite teaching specimen: coarse pale crystals and dark flecks form an irregular mosaic. This is one specimen, not every appearance of granite.
images.alt: Smithsonian granite specimen with a coarse mosaic of pale crystals and dark mineral flecks beside a centimeter scale.
images.credit: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History
images.context: Museum teaching specimen, not documented as a river find. No collecting locality supplied on the record.
images.licenseEvidence: Exact Smithsonian object page inspected in browser. Selected media carries CC0 Creative Commons - No Rights Reserved button; opened tooltip explicitly says this media is public domain and may be copied, modified and distributed without contacting Smithsonian. Verified selected first image URL through page DOM and download control when available; did not infer image rights from metadata license.

images.caption: Diorite hand specimen from near Azusa, California. Pale plagioclase and dark hornblende make the medium-grained speckled texture; the source identifies the specimen as 10 cm across.
images.alt: Diorite hand specimen showing strongly contrasting pale mineral grains and black hornblende against a black background.
images.credit: Joseph Hartman / Geoscience Digital Image Library
images.context: Photographed hand specimen, 10cm across according to source; not documented as a river find.
images.licenseEvidence: Exact image page HTML contains a copyright row linking CC0 1.0 with zero.svg license icon. GeoDIL copyright page warns not all images are freely licensed, so this image-specific license was checked; Commons independently records CC0 and source review on18August2026.

images.caption: Basalt from the Smithsonian teaching collection, Hawaii. Look for the dark, fine-grained material and cavities; many basalts are more compact than this example.
images.alt: Dark basalt teaching specimen with a fine-grained surface, ropy upper surface and visible cavities beside a centimeter scale.
images.credit: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History
images.context: Museum teaching specimen from Hawaii; not documented as a river find. Record describes three objects; caption refers only to this photographed basalt.
images.licenseEvidence: Exact Smithsonian object page inspected in browser. Selected media carries CC0 Creative Commons - No Rights Reserved button; opened tooltip explicitly says this media is public domain and may be copied, modified and distributed without contacting Smithsonian. Verified selected first image URL through page DOM and download control when available; did not infer image rights from metadata license.

images.caption: Sandstone teaching specimen from West Virginia. Its fine granular surface and subtle layers are useful clues; use the enlarged image to examine the grains.
images.alt: Tan sandstone specimen with a fine granular texture and subtle darker layers, with an original centimeter scale at the right.
images.credit: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History
images.context: Museum teaching specimen collected at U.S.Route48 north of Quarry Run, MonongaliaCounty, WestVirginia; not described as river-worn.
images.licenseEvidence: Exact Smithsonian object page inspected in browser. Selected media carries CC0 Creative Commons - No Rights Reserved button; opened tooltip explicitly says this media is public domain and may be copied, modified and distributed without contacting Smithsonian. Verified selected first image URL through page DOM and download control when available; did not infer image rights from metadata license.

images.caption: Gneiss in the field: pale and dark mineral bands run through a slab beside the Ryan Mountain Trail in Joshua Tree National Park. The USGS identifies the pale fracture fillings as aplite; this is not a river-worn specimen.
images.alt: Broad gneiss slab with closely spaced pale and dark bands, crosscut by pale fractures; a cell phone rests on its surface.
images.context: Field photograph of a slab beside a trail. Not identified as river-worn and not a museum hand specimen.
images.licenseEvidence: The exact USGS media record has a Sources/Usage section stating Public Domain. No separate photographer is identified on this record.

images.caption: Mica-rich Manhattan Schist, a collection specimen from New York. Shiny flakes and thin, wavy aligned surfaces illustrate its foliated texture; the source identifies muscovite, biotite and quartz.
images.alt: Gray mica-rich Manhattan Schist specimen with numerous reflective flakes and thin wavy layers; collection labels read 79.
images.credit: Mike Davis / GeoDIL, Ward’s Collection of Classic North American Rocks #79
images.context: Identified collection hand specimen. Not documented as a river find.
images.licenseEvidence: Downloaded exact specimen HTML contains a copyright row linking https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/ with the zero.svg license icon. The GeoDIL copyright policy explicitly distinguishes its CC0 photographs from restricted photographs; this image has its own CC0 icon.

images.caption: Fine-grained Baraboo Quartzite from Wisconsin, a collection specimen. Its pinkish-gray, granular-looking broken surface is one quartzite appearance; other quartzites may be white, gray or differently colored.
images.alt: Angular pinkish-gray Baraboo Quartzite specimen with a fine granular-looking surface and original collection labels numbered 76.
images.credit: Mike Davis / GeoDIL, Ward’s Collection of Classic North American Rocks #76
images.context: Identified collection hand specimen. Not documented as river-worn.
images.licenseEvidence: Downloaded exact specimen HTML contains its own copyright row linking https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/ with the zero.svg license icon. Corroborated by the exact GeoDIL #328 file record on Wikimedia Commons, which identifies this image as CC0.

images.caption: Calcite-rich marble from New York’s Adirondack lowlands, a collection specimen. Pale, closely packed crystals give this example a coarse sugary texture, with a few darker specks.
images.alt: Pale gray-white marble hand specimen with conspicuous crystalline grains, scattered dark specks, and original labels numbered 173.
images.credit: Nessa Eull / GeoDIL, Ward’s University Rock Collection #173
images.context: Identified collection hand specimen. Not documented as river-worn.
images.licenseEvidence: Downloaded exact specimen HTML contains its own copyright row linking https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/ with the zero.svg license icon. Exact Wikimedia Commons GeoDIL #506 file record also identifies CC0 and documents license review on 18 August 2026.

images.caption: Limestone reference specimen, Smithsonian NMNH 91536, from Inyo County, California. Notice the pale, fine-grained surface and narrow intersecting grooves; this is a collection specimen, not a river find.
images.alt: Pale fine-grained limestone specimen with narrow intersecting grooves and a darker side, on a dark background.
images.credit: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History, NMNH 91536 (CC0)
images.context: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History reference specimen, Inyo County, California. Not documented as a river find.
images.licenseEvidence: Individual object record states Viewer Image Usage: Creative Commons Zero and Open Access Online Media: Creative Commons Zero, followed by permission to copy, modify, and distribute. First viewer image was followed directly from that record, not inferred from general museum metadata.

images.caption: A different limestone example: coral fossils in the St. Louis Limestone near Blue Spring, Kentucky. The closely packed fossil outlines interrupt the fine-grained rock; many limestones do not show fossils this clearly.
images.alt: Close view of pale limestone containing many closely packed rounded fossil coral outlines.
images.context: Close-up of coral-bearing limestone at the documented Kentucky locality, view parallel to corallites. No river transport asserted.
images.licenseEvidence: The individual record contains a copyright table row linking to https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/ with the zero.svg license icon. This was checked in the actual downloaded HTML; GeoDIL copyright policy explicitly says some images are not freely licensed, so the per-image icon, not the site alone, is the approval evidence.

images.caption: Quartz mineral reference specimen from near Cripple Creek, Colorado, about 5 cm long. The crystal has a point at each end and visible faces; it is not a photographed river pebble.
images.alt: Creamy translucent quartz crystal with a point at each end, broad crystal faces, and rusty spots against black.
images.context: Photographed mineral reference specimen; not a documented river find.

images.caption: Pale chert from near Joplin, Missouri, about 9 cm across. The curved broken surfaces and very fine texture are useful clues; other cherts can be red, brown, gray, or nearly black.
images.alt: Pale cream and gray chert hand specimen with curved shell-like broken surfaces and two collection labels.
images.context: Collection hand specimen with labels; not a documented river find.

images.caption: Greenstone reference specimen from near Ely, Minnesota, 8 cm across. Notice the greenish-gray, fine-grained rock; individual minerals cannot be identified by eye in this example. This is a different locality from Shenandoah.
images.alt: Greenish-gray fine-grained greenstone hand specimen with pale narrow streaks and a blue collection label marked 198.
images.context: Collection hand specimen. Not Shenandoah material and not a documented river find.
